flowerLanguage: Perseverance, hope, and quiet strength in adversity.
history: Cultivated in China for over 3,000 years, the plum blossom is one of the 'Three Friends of Winter' alongside pine and bamboo. It is the unofficial national flower of China and the official city flower of Nanjing.
symbolism: Because it blooms in the depths of winter before any leaves appear, it symbolizes resilience and the triumph of spirit over hardship. Its five petals represent the five blessings: longevity, prosperity, health, virtue, and a peaceful death.
funFact: Nanjing's Plum Blossom Hill (梅花山) holds tens of thousands of plum trees and hosts an annual festival drawing visitors from across China.
careTip: Plum trees bloom best after a cold winter — the chill is what triggers their spring display.

flowerLanguage: Love, romance, and the irresistible pull of attraction.
history: Treasured in China for more than 2,500 years, osmanthus flowers have long been used to scent tea, wine, and sweets. The phrase 'plucking osmanthus from the moon palace' once described passing the imperial examinations.
symbolism: Its tiny blossoms carry an outsized fragrance, making it a symbol of nobility and true worth that needs no show. It is associated with the Mid-Autumn Festival and family reunion.
funFact: Osmanthus blooms are tiny and easy to miss — you almost always smell them long before you see them.
careTip: Plant near a path or window: the autumn fragrance is the whole point.

history: Sacred across Asia for millennia, the lotus appears throughout Buddhist and Taoist art. Confucian scholar Zhou Dunyi's essay 'On the Love of the Lotus' praised it as the flower of the virtuous gentleman.
symbolism: Rising clean and unstained from muddy water, the lotus represents spiritual purity and the soul's journey toward enlightenment. Every part of the plant is useful, a model of generosity.
funFact: Lotus seeds can remain viable for over a thousand years — one germinated seed was dated to roughly 1,300 years old.
careTip: Lotus needs full sun and still water; it will not bloom in shade.

history: Known in Chinese as 'Zhuge cai' (Zhuge's vegetable), legend ties it to the strategist Zhuge Liang, who is said to have had his troops plant it as a fast-growing food crop on campaign.
symbolism: Its carpets of pale violet blooms across early-spring parks and roadsides make it a symbol of cheerful, undemanding renewal.
funFact: The young leaves and shoots are edible — a genuine wild spring green still foraged in parts of China.
careTip: Self-seeds readily; let a few flowers go to seed and it returns every spring.

history: Grown across China for its oil-rich seeds for centuries, blooming rapeseed fields have become a spring tourism phenomenon, drawing travelers to golden landscapes from Jiangsu to Yunnan.
symbolism: Endless seas of yellow flowers symbolize prosperity, a good harvest, and the simple happiness of the countryside in spring.
funFact: The pressed seeds yield canola/rapeseed oil — one of the most widely used cooking oils in the world.
careTip: A cool-season crop; sow in autumn for a brilliant spring bloom.

flowerLanguage: Fidelity and a fond farewell — 'safe travels.'
history: Originally from western Asia, this tiny blue wildflower has naturalized across the temperate world. In Chinese it is affectionately called 'po po na,' a grandmotherly name.
symbolism: The English name 'speedwell' is a wish for a good journey. Its sky-blue blooms are among the first signs that spring has arrived.
funFact: Each flower lasts only a single day, dropping its petals by evening.
careTip: A lawn and field volunteer — no care needed; just don't mow too early in spring.

flowerLanguage: Abundant beauty and the fullness of celebration.
history: 'Kanzan' (also romanized Sekiyama) is a celebrated Japanese flowering cherry cultivar, prized for its dense, deep-pink double blossoms and widely planted in parks and avenues across East Asia.
symbolism: Where the single cherry whispers of fleeting beauty, the lush double Kanzan shouts of generosity and festive abundance — a flower made for crowds and celebration.
funFact: Each blossom can carry 20 to 50 petals, so heavy the branches droop under their own bloom.
careTip: Blooms slightly later than single cherries, extending the sakura season by a week or two.

history: Cultivated in Chinese temple gardens since the Tang dynasty, the 'Yulan' magnolia was once planted at the grounds of emperors. It is the official city flower of Shanghai.
symbolism: Its pure-white, candle-like blooms opening on bare branches symbolize purity of heart and noble character. It was historically a gift of high esteem.
funFact: Magnolias are ancient — they evolved before bees existed and are pollinated mainly by beetles.
careTip: Flowers appear before the leaves; a late frost can brown the petals, so shelter from cold winds.

flowerLanguage: The fleeting beauty of life; gentle transience.
history: Beloved throughout East Asia, the cherry blossom is the centerpiece of springtime flower-viewing. Nanjing's Jiming Temple road and Yuhuatai are famous local viewing spots.
symbolism: Because the bloom is so brief, it has come to represent mono no aware — a tender awareness of impermanence and the preciousness of the present moment.
funFact: A cherry tree's full bloom typically lasts only about one week before the petals fall like snow.
careTip: Best viewed on a still day — a single windy afternoon can end the bloom.

flowerLanguage: Quiet contribution and renewal of the earth.
history: For centuries Chinese farmers have sown milk vetch as a winter cover crop, plowing it under in spring as green manure to enrich rice paddies before planting.
symbolism: Its name 'purple cloud blossom' captures the rosy haze it casts over spring fields. It symbolizes the unseen, nourishing work that makes later abundance possible.
funFact: As a legume it fixes nitrogen from the air into the soil, naturally fertilizing the next season's crop — and it's a favorite of honeybees.
careTip: Sow in autumn as a cover crop; turn it into the soil at peak bloom for the richest green manure.
